messages.subject: overestimated standard deviation of random effect
parts:
Hi all

I think is is more of a general question, since I find this happening in both Stan and JAGS.

I am estimating a model with random effects, where a random effect is N(mean= -0.1, sd= .1). The problem is that the model consistently overestimates the sd, where the 95% CI doesnt inlcude the population sd= .1. I am using diffuse priors and the sample size is 50. Is it expected that the sd is overestimated when sd is this low or more informative priors should fix this issue?

Thank you for your help

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] overestimated standard deviation of random effect
parts:
Let’s assume that you’re using a uniform prior on
the standard deviation of the hierarchical distribution.
For sd = 0.1, there is finite mass below but infinite
mass above, hence the prior will bias the fit high.
For sd = 1 the same thing happens.  In fact, for
any finite value of sd there is infinite mass above
that value which can bias the fit high.  In other
words, “diffuse” priors aren’t actually uninformative,
they actually impose a huge amount of information
that large values are okay.  

What you are seeing in an issue of incoherency
where that prior bias towards large values is
inconsistent with your prior knowledge that the
sd has a reasonable value.  So you’ll need a
prior that is consistent with that knowledge,
for example a half Cauchy or half Normal
with scale on the order of the variation you’d
expect in the population.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] overestimated standard deviation of random effect
parts:
That is confusing. Why doesn't anyone indent? That's
a serious question --- we just get file after file from
people with no indentation at all and no spacing, which
makes these programs really hard to scan.

I'd recommend:

* just defining LGC3 directly rather than by constructing J
full of zeroes and multiplying (lots of useless multiply adds,
which are relatively slow).

* vectorizing the definitions of mu (just over i if that's
all that's possible --- I didn't slog through the actual definitions).

* don't use N and n as constants and then define N x n structures
(this is taste more than anything else)

* and speaking of taste, please, please, indent --- I don't know how
anyone can read or work with all this non-indented code --- it's
very hard to scan

* vectorize

for(j in 1:N){
X[j] ~ normal(mu[j], sd_x );
}

as

to_vector(X) ~ normal(to_vector(mu), sd_x);

by definining X to be a matrix.

- Bob
